newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Labour votes, Barak seen taking helm.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Labour votes, Barak seen taking helm.

text.p: Israel's main opposition Labour party, eager to oust Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government, voted on Tuesday for a new leader with ex-army chief Ehud Barak tipped to succeed Shimon Peres at the helm.

The leadership vote marked a milestone for Labour, a passing of the political torch from former prime minister Peres, 73, and his slain predecessor Yitzhak Rabin, whose rival camps ruled the often contentious party for nearly a quarter-century.
The heavily favoured Barak, 55, has cast himself as heir to Rabin's warrior-turned-peacemaker mantle.
"I see myself as his follower and the one to continue his legacy," Barak told a news conference on Monday.
The winner of the Tuesday contest is expected to face Netanyahu in national elections scheduled for 2000.

Echoing Rabin, who spearheaded Arab-Israeli talks until an ultra-nationalist Jew gunned him down after a 1995 peace rally, Barak said Labour was "committed to take calculated risks in the Middle East in order to achieve peace".

The voting closes at 1900 GMT and exit polls are expected to predict the winner soon afterwards. Only the 167,000 registered Labour Party members can vote. The winner must receive at least 40 percent of the vote.
Opinion polls have shown Barak neck and neck with the Likud party's Netanyahu, 47, whose first year in office has been buffeted by peacemaking crises and clouded by corruption allegations.
"The Labour party has gotten back up on its feet and a journey has begun which is perhaps long but which will in the end return us to leading the country," Barak told Israel Radio on Tuesday.

Facing Barak are Peres's longtime protege Yossi Beilin, 48, the bookish prophet of Labour peace policies; Shlomo Ben-Ami, 53, a Moroccan-born novice politician with roots both in academia and among the disadvantaged; and Ephraim Sneh, 52, a physician and brigadier general before he served Rabin and Peres as health minister.

Barak joined Labour barely two years ago after shedding the uniform of Israel's most decorated soldier. Long before entering public life, Barak was a near-legendary military figure -- bold, aloof, and brilliant. He was Netanyahu's commander when both served in an elite commando unit.
The military credentials have helped catapault self-described centrist Barak to prominence in a country where security remains the paramount -- if not the sole -- issue in election campaigns.
Barak joined Rabin's cabinet as interior minister in 1995, succeeding Peres as foreign minister when the Labour veteran took the reins of government following the Rabin assassination.
Netanyahu edged Peres in an upset election victory in 1996, in part by characterising the Nobel peace laureate as soft on security.
Labour's primary campaign has been called unusually gentlemanly, the candidates mindful of avoiding the infighting that kept the party in the electoral cold for much of the last two decades.
The relative calm was broken last month, when Barak's forces quashed a bid by Peres's backers to appoint the veteran leader honorary party president. Peres has stayed out of the fray.
